# Psalm 137: verse-by-verse research notes

**Gaps:** I couldn't find anything on Psalm 137 from Lutheran, Pentecostal or Methodist denominational websites (lcms.org, 1517.org, ag.org, seedbed.com, wesley.nnu.edu). Instead I've used each tradition's classic commentators where they appeared on biblehub or studylight: Adam Clarke (Methodist), Keil & Delitzsch (Lutheran), Gill and Spurgeon (Baptist), Calvin (Reformed). I found nothing from bibleodyssey.org, catholic.com, or prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching on this psalm, so none of that is included. Several pages I tried to open in full didn't load, so some notes rest on search-result excerpts only. Catholic and Orthodox Bibles number this psalm 136.

---

**Whole psalm / setting**
- Guzik says many commentators think it was written after the return from exile, though it could come from many years into the exile. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-137/
- Calvin (Reformed) says it is "a great mistake" to think David wrote it as a prophecy of the coming exile. In his view it describes the exile as something that had already happened. https://www.ccel.org/c/calvin/comment3/comm_vol12/htm/xxi.htm
- bible.org notes that every verb in vv. 1–3 is in the Hebrew perfect tense. That may mean the writer lived after the exile and was looking back on it. https://bible.org/seriespage/psalm-137
- Spurgeon (Baptist) points out that the psalm asking "How can we sing?" is itself a song of the Lord. https://studylight.org/commentaries/tod/psalms-137.html
- NET Bible summary: the exiles mourn their condition, vow loyalty to Jerusalem, and ask God for revenge on their enemies. http://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Psa&chapter=137

**v. 1**
- The river was probably the Euphrates. Israel had no river that large, and its size told the exiles they were no longer home. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-137/
- Guzik lists the reasons they wept: loved ones dead, Jerusalem and the temple destroyed, cruel captors, and their own sin that brought the judgment. He also quotes Boice: the Hebrew ending *nu* ("we/our") comes nine times in vv. 1–3 and sounds like a moan. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-137/
- bible.org suggests "waterways" may be the better translation, because Babylon had man-made canals as well as rivers. https://bible.org/seriespage/psalm-137
- Clarke (Methodist), quoted by Guzik: Jews in exile often met for worship by rivers (compare Acts 16:13). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-137/
- Augustine (Catholic): believers should "sit by" the waters of Babylon, meaning the passing pleasures of this world, and weep humbly rather than plunge in. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801137.htm

**v. 2**
- Calvin: the psalmist is mourning that the temple praise God had commanded has stopped. The pleasant shade of the willows could not ease grief that deep. https://www.ccel.org/c/calvin/comment3/comm_vol12/htm/xxi.htm
- Gill (Baptist): the speakers were probably temple Levites who had saved their harps from the plunder, hoping to use them again. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/137-2.html
- Matthew Henry: they hung the harps where they could see them, not hidden. But he wonders whether they were wrong to stop, since praising God is never out of season. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/137-2.html
- Boice, quoted by Guzik: they didn't smash the harps but saved them for a better day. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-137/
- bible.org: the "willow" was probably a kind of poplar that grows along the Euphrates. https://bible.org/seriespage/psalm-137
- Augustine, an allegory: the harps stand for the Scriptures and God's promises. The willows are fruitless people fed by worldly pleasure, and the harps are hung up rather than used on them. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801137.htm

**v. 3**
- The people who had plundered them now wanted entertainment, but the exiles had no song left. Guzik quotes Kidner on an Assyrian carving that shows prisoners playing lyres under guard. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-137/
- Fr. Lawrence Farley (Orthodox) calls the request "the crowning humiliation": temple hymns turned into something like a pagan drinking song. https://www.oca.org/reflections/fr.-lawrence-farley/by-the-waters-of-babylon
- bible.org: the Hebrew word for "tormentors" appears only here in the Bible. https://bible.org/seriespage/psalm-137
- Augustine: Christians are captives too, tempted by earthly pleasures, and Christ is the one who redeems them from the devil. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801137.htm

**v. 4**
- These songs came out of the people's relationship with God. They were not entertainment, so they could not be performed for oppressors. G. Campbell Morgan, quoted by Guzik, says singing them would have meant betraying Jerusalem. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-137/
- F. B. Meyer, quoted by Guzik, applies the verse to Christians: when we lose our song, disobedience is often the cause. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-137/
- The devotional notes in Spurgeon's *Treasury of David* apply it the same way: when a believer falls into sin, the harp goes on the willows. https://studylight.org/commentaries/tod/psalms-137.html

**vv. 5–6**
- The singer curses himself if he forgets: his hand would lose its skill on the harp and his tongue its ability to sing. Guzik quotes VanGemeren: Jerusalem stood for covenant, temple, God's presence, atonement and forgiveness. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-137/
- Spurgeon: here the psalm moves from "we" to "I", so each exile makes the vow personally. https://studylight.org/commentaries/tod/psalms-137.html
- bible.org calls it a self-curse used for literary intensity, and a sign of faith in dark times. https://bible.org/seriespage/psalm-137
- Trapp, quoted by Guzik, describes a Jewish custom of leaving part of a new house unfinished in memory of Jerusalem's ruin. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-137/
- Orthodox application (Farley): Christians also live in "Babylon" and should put Jerusalem above their highest joy. https://www.oca.org/reflections/fr.-lawrence-farley/by-the-waters-of-babylon

**v. 7**
- When God "remembers" here, it means he opposes and judges. The Edomites came from Esau, Jacob's brother, and should have stood with Jerusalem. Instead they enjoyed its fall (compare Obadiah). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-137/
- VanGemeren, quoted by Guzik: "foundations" means God's whole rule on earth, not just the city walls. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-137/
- Constable: the psalmist vowed to remember Jerusalem, and now he asks God to remember its destroyers. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/137-7.html
- bible.org: when God remembers, it is usually in judgment. The Jewish Publication Society translation reads "strip her, strip her", the picture of a woman publicly shamed. https://bible.org/seriespage/psalm-137

**v. 8**
- Guzik notes that, unlike v. 7, this is not a prayer to God. He suggests the psalmist saw Babylon's judgment as so certain that it only needed announcing. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-137/
- Keil & Delitzsch (Lutheran), a word study: the Hebrew can mean "must be laid waste." A Semitic curse pictures the future as already done. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/137-9.htm
- Augustine: "daughter of Babylon" works like "daughter of Zion" or "daughter of the Church", naming a city that succeeds another. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801137.htm

**v. 9**
*The traditional reading: a call for God's justice, matching what Babylon did*
- Gill (Baptist): this was fair payback, since Babylon had done the same to Jewish children and Isaiah 13:16 foretold it. He says it comes from zeal for God's justice, not revenge. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/137-9.htm
- Keil & Delitzsch (Lutheran): killing the children would stop a new generation from rebuilding Babylon's power, and "zeal for God" lies behind the harsh words. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/137-9.htm
- Clarke (Methodist): Babylon was so oppressive and hated that those who destroyed it would be praised. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/137-9.html
- Matthew Henry: if the little ones die, Babylon's ruin is final as well as complete. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/137-9.html
- Ligonier (Reformed): the Old Testament often sees an enemy as needing to be destroyed completely. It also says the Edomites had done this very thing to Israel's children. https://learn.ligonier.org/podcasts/ask-ligonier/how-should-christians-view-the-imprecatory-psalms
- GotQuestions: this is not a selfish prayer for personal revenge. It asks God to keep his covenant and set things right. https://www.gotquestions.org/dashing-babies-against-rocks.html
- Spurgeon, quoted by Guzik: critics who have never seen their children killed might be less "velvet-mouthed." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-137/

*Where Protestant teachers really differ*
- **Barnes (Presbyterian)** admits the verse does seem to approve the act. It "savors more of imprecation than forgiveness." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/137-9.htm
- **Coffman (Church of Christ)** says a curse on helpless children goes against Christ's word, though it reflects how ancient wars were fought. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/137-9.html
- **Boice (Presbyterian)**, quoted by Guzik: since the cross, our calling is to pray for reconciliation, not judgment. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-137/
- **C. S. Lewis (Anglican)**, as described by Trevin Wax at TGC: Lewis called these psalms "devilish" and ruled out curses on human enemies for Christians. Wax thinks Lewis got this wrong. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/blogs/trevin-wax/cs-lewis-cursing-psalms/
- **Paul Carter (TGC Canada)** sees no real difference between this prayer and the martyrs' cry in Revelation 6:9–11. He also cites Motyer's translation "How *right*" in place of "blessed." https://ca.thegospelcoalition.org/columns/ad-fontes/dashing-little-ones-rock-verse-really-belong-scripture/

*Allegory (Catholic, rejected by some Protestants)*
- Augustine: Babylon's "little ones" are sinful desires as they first appear. They should be dashed on the "rock", which he takes to be Christ, before they grow into habits. https://www.ccel.org/ccel/schaff/npnf108.ii.CXXXVII.html
- Gill knows this reading and rejects it: it "seems to have no place here." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/137-9.htm

*Notes on the words*
- Ellicott: "little ones" literally means "sucklings", and "stones" is better translated "cliff" or "rock." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/137-9.htm
- bible.org: "the rock" has "the" in front of it. It might refer to Petra in Edom, or to idols set against God, "the true Rock." https://bible.org/seriespage/psalm-137

*Orthodox use in worship*
- The Orthodox Church sings this psalm at Matins on the three Sundays before Lent, starting with the Sunday of the Prodigal Son, to stress the theme of exile. https://www.oca.org/saints/lives/2025/02/16/3-sunday-of-the-prodigal-son
